1.​Introduction
1.1 Saoloto - The Origin
During Genesis at our surf school, the ultimate objective was to guarantee
a genuineness whose equal has never been seen.
This obsession with creating a “brand” with these levels of focus on what is
genuine and authentic requires a name as authentic as the space, the teaching and the “Vibes”.
The surfing that this school aims to promote is strongly influenced by the roots of
surfing, which the world saw born in 400 AD on the sands of French Polynesia, a sport that
was once considered the sport of kings, which in the 12th century was already represented in
cave paintings in the form of He’e Nalu (Booth, n.d.).
A form of expression that saw its existence threatened upon the arrival of
European missionaries on the continent in 1820, who considered the activity as lazy and
a waste of time and had to wait until the end of the 20th century to see its
popularity resurfaced by the "Beach Boys of Waikiki", Duke Kahanamoku (The father of
modern surfing) in particular (Soft Surfboards®, n.d.).
The only thing we knew was that the name would have to be authentically Polynesian
(original language of surfing), it would have to be a word that represented the core value of the
surfing and he would have to ensure that no one who heard him could remain indifferent to him.
It would have to immediately convey a clear message about what, as a school,
we value; would have to be representative of the essence we look for in all the people we meet.
they look for us; it would have to honor all the figures and cultures that brought surfing to us; would have
above all, represent the feeling of freedom that these heroes have always fought for
preserve.
It would have to be Freedom.
It would have to be Saoloto.
1.2 The Project
The present work aims to propose a go-to-market strategy
(GTM) for a surf school located in Costa de Caparica, Saoloto Surf School. For
To this end, the development of the project was structured into three distinct moments.
In a first phase, a comprehensive analysis was carried out, focusing on
either on the school's external environment, including the market, both nationally and
international level, competition, target audience and surf culture, whether on the environment
internal, centered on the organization itself.
As Saoloto Surf School is a fictitious brand, the internal analysis showed
limitations in terms of available information, which led to the second phase of the project: the
creation of the brand and the development of the respective brand guidelines. At this stage, there were
elements of a strategic and emotional nature are addressed, such as the Golden Circle, as well as
more operational components, such as the marketing mix, among other fundamental elements
for the structure and coherence of the project.
The objective was to build a true “bible” of the brand,
fundamental to guarantee an identity and communication differentiated from the competition,
supported by the consistency and coherence that this type of model provides.
Finally, considering that the curricular unit focuses on campaign strategy,
the brand's ecosystem was developed and, consequently, all pieces of
communication considered relevant to a project whose purpose is market entry.
In this way, the work presents a structure with a beginning, middle and end, seeking
address the main critical points of an organized go-to-market strategy,
based on each decision made and, above all, aligned with the needs of the
market, target audience and business logic.

2.1.2 - Market Analysis
Market analysis constitutes a fundamental step in defining a
effective go-to-market strategy, as it allows understanding the context in which
the brand you want to insert. Through this analysis, it is possible to identify trends,
opportunities and constraints in the sector, as well as evaluating the behavior of the
consumer, competitive dynamics and external factors that influence demand.
In the context of this project, market analysis assumes particular relevance
for supporting strategic decisions related to the positioning of Saoloto Surf
School, ensuring that the value proposition, communication and marketing actions are
aligned with the real needs of the market and the expectations of the target audience.
2.1.2.1 Market - Surfing
Surfing is an activity with a long history, whose origins date back to 400 AD,
as already mentioned. Over time, it was adopted by different cultures and evolved until it became
become a global practice. Therefore, it is a widely consolidated market at a
international, its analysis must consider this broad dimension. However, given that the
Saoloto Surf School will be based in Portugal, it is equally essential to read the
national reality.
The main challenge lies in access to updated data: many studies are
pre-pandemic, some reports are not public and the most recent statistics show
significant gaps between them. Thus, whenever information about Portugal is non-existent
or insufficient, this absence will be explained, using available data, such as
form of contextualization, even though these may lack precision for the current scenario.
Despite these limitations, the articulation between global and national analysis allows
understand the level of competitiveness, the existing offer and the possible positioning for
Saoloto, aspects that will be deepened and complemented in the analysis of the competition. A
international level, we seek above all to understand what stage the market is at, whether
it is one of expansion, innovation or stabilization based on tradition. This framework will be
fundamental to assess the growth potential of Saoloto Surf School.
Starting from this analytical framework, we then proceed to characterize the
global surfing market.
The available data present very different estimates regarding the
total number of active surfers in the world. The most recent reference, dated 2024,
continues to use the 2012 estimate, which pointed to around 35 million practitioners
(Armstrong & Dickerson, 2024). The lack of updated numbers may be related
with the very informality and fluidity of surf culture, which suggests that the real value may
be currently higher, especially considering recent growth trends
(discussed in point 2.1.2.6 - trends) .
The reliability of these numbers remains limited because the concept of “surfer
asset” is not defined consistently across different sources. One of the few
explicit definitions, presents a distinction between a “casual” surfer, understood as
“anyone who has surfed at least once during the year”, and a “core” surfer,
described as “someone who surfed more than eight times during the year” (STAB, 2016). No
However, it is not possible to confirm whether the remaining sources adopt these same criteria, a
since they do not clarify how they classify practitioners. Therefore, it is not known whether an individual
who owns a board but hardly uses it, or someone who only surfs a few times
per year, is counted in the same way as a regular practitioner. These ambiguities
make it difficult to precisely define the target audience and highlight the need for Saoloto
collect own data over time, in order to build a more detailed characterization
reliable and suited to the reality of your market.
Continuing the analysis, according to existing estimates, of the 35 million
surfers, around 13.5 million are in North and South America, 6.5 million in Oceania,
6 million in Asia and 4.5 million in Europe. In terms of countries, the United States counts
with approximately 3 million practitioners, Australia with 1.7 million and the United Kingdom
United with around 500 thousand. Portugal appears in sixth European position, with
approximately 200 thousand surfers (Pinto, n.d.).
Discrepancies are equally notable in the estimated value of the global market.
One of the sources points to 9.82 billion euros in 2025, with annual growth
6.3% by 2032 (Coherent Market Insights, 2025); another estimates 71.93 billion,
predicting growth of 12.3% by 2035, potentially reaching 157.56 billion
(Future Marketing Insight, 2025). Despite the differences, both confirm a tendency towards
consistent expansion, driven by several factors that will be explored later.
In the case of Portugal, projections suggest a market valued at 2,344 million
of dollars, with an estimated growth of 7.2% until 2030, the year in which it could reach
3,566 million. If these predictions are confirmed, Portugal will become, by the end of the
decade, the European country with the highest revenue in the sector, reinforcing the attractiveness of the market
national for new projects (Grand View Horizon, n.d.).
Regarding market segments, one of the first distinctions is between surf
domestic and international. Surfing practiced within the country represents between 68% and 71% of the
market share, which reveals a clear preference among consumers to remain in their
usual context, benefiting from lower costs, greater convenience and absence of
cultural barriers (Coherent Market Insights, 2025). International surfing, although it represents
around 30%, is also growing, particularly among practitioners
coming from countries without a consolidated surfing culture or without natural conditions
favorable. For foreign operators (such as Saoloto), these segments represent a
opportunity, since national competition does not exist, and they are more likely to
spend more money than locals (Future Marketing Insight, 2025).
In the Portuguese case (image 2 in the annex), there is no data indicating how many
of the 200 thousand surfers practice outside or only within the country, but existing data on
tourists who visit Portugal to surf, mostly Europeans, show a
relevant potential (Calheiros, 2018). Markets such as the United States or Australia,
from which surfing has historically expanded, remain underrepresented in tourism
surfing in Portugal, which opens up a strategic opportunity: either to attract surfers
originating from these markets, differentiating themselves from national competition, or to explore these
destinations at a later stage, when the brand has greater notoriety and authority.
With regard to the consumer profile, international data indicate that
around 65.8% of surfers are men, a value influenced by cultural factors and the
image historically associated with surfing (Coherent Market Insights, 2025). However, the
Women have risen to prominence, in part due to the growing influence of public figures and
content creators who promote more inclusive surfing. In terms of age, the group
between 26 and 35 years old represents approximately 40% of the market, a stage of life in which
there is a greater balance between financial capacity, physical availability and flexibility of
time (Future Marketing Insight, 2025).
In Portugal (image 2 in the annex), the most relevant data, even if dated
2018, suggest that 99% of practitioners are men, of which 78.6% are between 15 and 34 years old

As for women, although they represented less than 1% at the time, global growth
of this segment and the role of current influencers make them too relevant to be
ignored in Saoloto's communication.
Another segmentation criterion refers to the type of tourist. The market is divided between

approximately 61.9% (Coherent Market Insights, 2025). The groups are mostly
made up of beginners looking for structured, safe and convenient experiences,
characteristics that a school with a good reputation can guarantee. Travelers

In Portugal (image 3 in the annex), the period between October and April offers the best

provide ideal conditions, with warmer waters and a climate conducive to use

Despite the limitations of available data, much of which predates the pandemic,
all sources converge on one essential point: the global surfing market continues to grow,
and Portugal asserts itself as one of the main drivers of this expansion in Europe. It is

is today higher than that recorded in older studies.
Practitioners looking for international experiences, around 30% of the total,
represent a clear opportunity, especially those from landlocked or landlocked countries.
surfing tradition, like Germany, Switzerland or Austria. In Asia, China's growing interest
stands out as a sign of future potential (Coherent Market Insights, 2025). Markets
traditionally strong countries such as the United States and Australia maintain their strategic value,
although they may require a more differentiated approach due to strong local competition.
In behavioral terms, it is observed that beginners tend to join groups,
while experienced surfers mostly travel solo or in small groups, which
reinforces the importance of developing different products for each segment.
Finally, although the market continues to be predominantly male, the
growth in female participation transforms this segment into a relevant opportunity,
where inclusion and representation can constitute differentiating factors for Saoloto
Surf School.
2.1.2.2 Presentation of the Competition
Once the functioning of the market is understood, it becomes necessary to analyze the level of
competition. This analysis allows us to understand how different surf schools operate:
what products they offer, how they communicate and through what channels, among others
important points for the construction of the SSS. Therefore, the objective of this section is to provide a
solid basis for defining the pillars of the marketing mix and brand guidelines that
will distinguish Saoloto Surf School in the market.
Before proceeding to the analysis of selected competitors, it is important to justify the
changing the location initially planned for Saoloto, complementing it with a
overview of the panorama of surf schools in Portugal.
The original physical location defined for Saoloto was Cascais. However, after a
preliminary analysis, it became evident that this choice would not be suitable for the objectives
project strategies.
According to a specialized information agency (not a Portuguese body
official), there are approximately 678 surf schools in Portugal. The three regions with
The largest concentrations are: Costa da Caparica (62 schools), Ericeira (32) and Carcavelos (29).
Cascais only comes in ninth place, with 13 schools (PoiData.io, 2025).
At first glance, Cascais may seem like a more prestigious location, while
Costa da Caparica may seem less appealing. However, it is essential to analyze
only the absolute number of schools, but also the available coastal area and the way in which
These schools are distributed throughout this area.
Cascais has a coastline of around 30 kilometers (Cascais, n.d.).
However, a significant part of this coast does not correspond to beach areas. How is it
possible to check through Google maps (image 4 in the annex), much of the coastline is
composed of cliffs, cliffs, urban areas or marinas. The result is that Cascais has
only five beaches, relatively small and, in most cases, inserted in a context
urban, which limits the creation of a distinctive experience.
In contrast, Costa da Caparica presents characteristics more aligned with the
project proposal. The different sources consulted vary in terms of length
total coastline, estimated between 15 and 35 kilometers, but regardless of the exact value,
it is a coast made entirely of sand. As we move away from the
urban core (closer to Lisbon), the beaches become progressively more
surrounded by green areas, giving the place a more natural, wild and
less urban, even though the distance to the capital remains reduced (images 5 and 6 in the annex).
This distance also influences the distribution of schools: the greater the
distance from the central area, the lower the concentration of schools, as illustrated in image 7
of the annex. Observation of the spatial distribution confirms that the majority of schools
is concentrated in the initial section of the coast, close to the urban area, where they are located
lots of restaurants, shops, hotels and terminal points for various transport routes
public.
In this way, Costa da Caparica presents a large space for exploration, not
exploration that leads to the exchange of existing green space for something usable, which implies the
destruction of that same space, but for the construction of something that uses the space
environment as a “prop” to create an environment that matches surf culture,
culture, which will be explored later, in point 2.1.3 Analysis of Culture, which will serve as
also as reinforcement to justify this exchange between locations.
Having justified the future physical location of Saoloto, the next step is to present the
competition. This analysis was segmented into 3, direct, indirect and potential competition.
2.1.2.2.1 Direct Competition
Direct competition comprises entities that the brand identifies as a
immediate threat, as they operate in the same market, target the same target audience and
offer very similar services that satisfy the same needs. This typology of
competition explicitly competes for the attention, preference and purchasing decision of the
consumer.
For this analysis, three distinct brands were selected based on a criteria of
geographic diversification. With Saoloto aiming to capture the international market,
selection included references such as Outtheback (due to its strong external reach); the relevance
competitiveness of the Cascais hub justified the inclusion of a representative player of this
region; and finally, given the extent and importance of Costa da Caparica, the
competition from greater geographic proximity.
Below is a detailed contextualization of each:
2.1.2.2.1.1 Gecko Surf School (Costa da Caparica)
Link: https://geckosurfschool.com/en/
Gecko Surf School, founded in 2016, is a surf school located in Praia de
Santo António, in Costa da Caparica. The mission of this school is to provide experiences
memorable and transformative experiences through surfing, promoting connections with nature,
personal confidence and a healthy lifestyle (Gecko Surf School, n.d.). Offers classes for
beginners and advanced surfers, as well as equipment rental.
Competitiveness Relationship: This constitutes a direct threat due to its occupation
geographic location and ease of access for those looking to practice the sport in
close to Lisbon. Although its service portfolio does not fully reflect the
breadth that the Saoloto project intends to have (especially in terms of the Surf Camp
more structured), its strong local presence competes directly for the same segment of
students.
Strategic Challenge: The challenge for Saoloto here is not just technical, but also
perception of freshness: while Gecko is the "school as usual", Saoloto must position itself
as the "evolution of experience".
Critical Differentiation: Another observation concerns communication. Despite
mention that the connection with nature (Gecko Surf School, n.d.) is one of the pillars that
intend to provide as a brand, visual communication does not suggest this, very
probably due to the location that does not facilitate this connection. A point that at Saoloto
will be reinforced, due to the advantage that the recommended location provides to the project.
2.1.2.2.1.2 Surf Cascais (Cascais)
Link: https://www.surfcascais.com/pt
Surf Cascais is a surf school located in Cascais, whose product is
main the Surf Camp, a format that combines daily surf classes, accommodation in a
community and social activities, creating a total immersion in the surfing lifestyle.
The school offers classes for all levels, from beginners to surfers
intermediate courses, led by certified instructors.
The accommodation, known as Surf House, is a space located in Murches,
just minutes from the beaches of Cascais. It has a swimming pool, lounge areas, kitchen
shared rooms and rooms, designed to promote coexistence between surfers from different
nationalities and create a true community.
In addition to classes and accommodation, Surf Cascais also offers complete packages that
include transportation, breakfast, equipment rental and social events,
positioning itself as an ideal option for tourists and travelers looking for a
complete and carefree surfing experience.
Competitiveness Relationship: Surf Cascais stands out for the maturity of its
service ecosystem. Its strength lies in offering a range of highly
structured and complementary, which allow an effective upselling strategy (hosting
+ classes + social experiences). This ability to sell an integrated experience is very
similar to the value proposition planned for Saoloto Surf School, making them a
direct competitor in the dispute for the surf tourist's share of pocket.
Strategic Challenge: Saoloto's competitive advantage will lie in its narrative
brand and the "escapism" provided by the location. While Surf Cascais operates
In a more urban and conventional context, Saoloto differentiates itself through a
visual communication deeply linked to nature and the culture of freedom inspired by
Samoan spirit. The challenge is to position the project as a paradisiacal, humble and
disconnected from the pressure of the modern world. By transforming the privileged location into a
differentiation asset, Saoloto stops being just "another school" and becomes a
destination of authenticity, something that the more mass offer in Cascais cannot achieve
replicate.
2.1.2.2.1.3 Outtheback (New Zealand)
Link: https://www.outtheback.nz/
Based in the South Island of New Zealand, Outtheback (OTB) is a reference
international in teaching surfing in remote and difficult to access locations. Its offer focuses on
group surf camps and personalized trips that focus on exclusivity and contact
direct to the virgin nature of New Zealand's west and south coast.
Competitive Relationship: OTB is considered a direct competitor in the
plan of international reach. In the decision-making journey of an international tourist,
It is expected that the choice begins with selecting the destination and experience. Given that the
Saoloto aims to convert this foreign audience, the brand competes directly with
OTB for the attention of consumers searching for "authentic and
remote areas" worldwide.
Strategic Challenge: The challenge for Saoloto is to elevate its positioning to
that is perceived not only as a local option in Portugal, but as a
global authority in surf teaching. The OTB analysis allows us to identify good practices in
communication of "wild" destinations and the curation of private trips, serving as
inspiration for Saoloto to replicate this feeling of exclusivity and adventure in
South Bank.
Digital Differentiation: To compete with players of this caliber, Saoloto must
invest in an SEO and content marketing strategy that positions it as the alternative
European Union to the OTB model. The objective is to intercept the client in the planning phase,
demonstrating that it is possible to find the same philosophy of freedom and "remote places"
just minutes from a European capital, such as Lisbon.
These are some examples of direct competing brands. As stated, they were
chosen based on a geographical criterion, but among different possibilities, these were
those chosen because they demonstrate the path that Saoloto will follow.
Gecko represents the importance of a sense of community and implementation
location. As the community is one of the most valuable assets in the surfing market, Gecko serves as a
example on how to create close bonds with the practitioner.
Surf Cascais is proof of concept that, in Portugal, it is possible to operate a
structured and profitable project. It represents the level of operational maturity that Saoloto
aims to achieve, serving as a basis for the development of its processes.
Outtheback functions as the aspirational horizon. Its global reach and
brand authority are Saoloto's long-term objective, positioning it not only
as a local school, but as a reference in the global market of learning experiences
surfing.
Finally, it is important to mention that in continuous work with the brand, this analysis must
be more extensive, not only in terms of analyzing these brands, but also others, since
that the objective will always be to stand out in the market, and in terms of business objective, to sell
as many vacancies as possible, every year. For academic purposes, these were examples
of direct competition.

Saoloto: The Strength of the Tribe at Sea
Common World: Contemporary surfing has become a sport of
isolation. Schools focus on individual performance, on the technique of "me" against the wave.

stage for your ego and personal achievement. It is unknown that, in Samoan origins, surfing

dangerous. When we separate the surfer from his environment and peers, we lose the essence
spirituality of practice. We forget that treating the ocean as an object separates us from
nature, and treating surfing as an isolated achievement separates us from humanity. Without the
connection to the whole, the technique is empty and the surfer remains incomplete.
Solution: Saoloto Surf School recovers the ancestral perspective: we don't surf
in the ocean, you surf with him and with others. Our pedagogy goes beyond maneuvering;
we build an experience where the student learns to breathe in unison with the tide and the
group. We teach that the wave does not belong to anyone, it is shared, just like the energy that
moves us.
Transformation: We restore the lost link between man, the gods and the
group. The big lesson is the Samoan paradox: only when someone truly becomes
part of a community is that it can rise up as an individual. At Saoloto, you are no longer
a solitary visitor at sea to become part of a living ecosystem, finding your
identity through belonging.

2.3.4.2 Monitoring and Optimization
2.3.4.2.1 Metrics
As the strategy is designed to cover the three phases of the consumer journey,
it is necessary that, in each of them, marketing efforts are analyzed, in order to
identify which tactics present positive results, which require adjustments and
that others can be explored to generate improvements.
Thus, the six metrics necessary for this exercise will be distributed in a
balanced by the three phases:
TOFU
CCR (Cultural Content Reach) - Cultural Content Reach,
specifically content that “leans in” to Saoloto’s Samoan roots.
BSV (Branded Search Volume) - Search Volume for terms such as:
Saoloto, Saoloto Surf School, Saoloto Surf, Saoloto School, etc… (Allows you to evaluate the level of
“awareness” that people have of the brand).
MOFU
AToP (Average Time on Page) - Average time visitors spend on
our page (or pages) allows us to perceive interest and at the same time evaluate the level of
optimization of these same pages.
CGR (Community Growth Rate) - Measures the percentage of growth of
subscribers in the "tribe" and loyalty channels (such as the Newsletter, Reddit or Groups
Private). Allows you to evaluate how many users are moving from being just observers to
become active members who want to belong to the Saoloto family.
BOFU
CVR (Conversion Rate) - The percentage of website visitors who
effectively finalize the purchase of a class or service. Being a new brand, this
metric is crucial to validating whether the “Samoan spirit” narrative is convincing enough
to lead to immediate commercial action.
CLV (Customer Lifetime Value) – The total monetary value a student generates
throughout their relationship with the school (recurring classes, rentals, merchandising, “Surf
Camps”). It is the fundamental metric to ensure that Saoloto is not just an attraction
“single use” tourist destination, but rather a brand that creates lasting relationships and loyalty.
2.3.4.2.2 Analysis Tools
For these metrics to be analyzed effectively, it is necessary to use
tools that make this process more practical. In this sense, those considered most
suitable for analyzing the metrics mentioned above, according to each phase of the funnel, are
the following:
Meta Business (+ Meta Ads) ➡️ CCR

in terms of reach and engagement due to its characteristics (DataReportal) is important
use the tools that Meta Business has to analyze the results of campaigns,
whether paid ads (Paid Media) or organic efforts (Owned Media).
Google Analytics (+ Looker Studio) ➡️ AToP; CVR; CLV
The website will be the central measurement platform for the entire marketing strategy.
Since conversions occur at the site level and traffic coming from other
platforms ends its journey at this point, it is essential that all analysis is concentrated
in a single tool, ensuring an integrated and coherent view of performance.
To achieve this, it will be necessary to build data bridges between platforms, through
of Google Tag Manager, a tool that allows you to implement and manage tracking code,
ensuring correct communication and data collection throughout the entire ecosystem
digital.
Google Search Console ➡️ BSV;
In order to understand how Saoloto Surf School is searched for on the internet, this
tool allows you to analyze the search terms used by users, the position
average of the brand's website in organic results and how these results
evolve over time. It is especially relevant for the analysis and optimization of
organic performance and website SEO strategy.
Mod Insights (“Community Health” dashboard) ➡️ CGR;
It is a native tool for the channel on Reddit, one of the platforms
used for the construction and management of the Saoloto community. This community is made up
by an audience that already understands the brand’s positioning and shows interest in
be part of your ecosystem.
The tool allows you to analyze the performance of publications on this network,
namely audience interactions, activity levels, community growth
and other relevant metrics to assess community health and engagement throughout
of time.
2.3.4.2.3 Diagnosis - Problems and Optimizations
This point aims to demonstrate the team’s critical capacity in
anticipate and mitigate potential problems, demonstrating a strategic vision that goes beyond the
idealized planning. Although the risk scenarios are varied, three were identified
possibilities for which Saoloto Surf School presents answers in advance
outlined.
1st Problem:
●​ AToP (Avg. Time on Page) very high on the "History" and "Legends" pages.
●​ Very low CVR (Conversion Rate).
Website visitors spend a fairly healthy amount of time on
pages that contain authentic and genuine content about the history and legends of surfing,
unfortunately the conversion rate remains very low.
Optimization: People are immersed in reading the Samoan spirit (which explains
time on the page high), but the site works like a museum: the user reads, gets inspired, and goes
although because the buy button disappeared up there.
Implement a "Sticky CTA Button" that floats on top or
bottom of the screen and follows the user's scroll. This ensures that the "Book
Class" is always visible at the exact moment the user feels inspired by the
story, without breaking the fluidity of reading.
2nd Problem:
●​ High CCR (Cultural Content Reach) and CGR (Community Growth).
●​ Low BSV (Branded Search Volume) in the school's local area.
In this situation, cultural content demonstrates solid performance. O
its consumption and distribution contribute positively to the growth of the community. No
However, this growth may occur mainly in international markets where the
Demand for surfing is not particularly high.
Even though Saoloto positions itself as an international school,
(considering that the language of surfing is universal) there are markets where the demand for
this practice is extremely limited. Thus, a community composed largely of
percentage by individuals coming from these markets will hardly translate into
conversions.
Optimization: The social platforms algorithm is optimizing the distribution of
content to where "taste" is cheaper and more abundant, ignoring the likelihood of
actual purchase. The budget is paying for vanity metrics in markets that do not
consume the product. Implement a "Negative Geo-Targeting" strategy (Exclusion
Geographic) in top-of-funnel campaigns.
Markets identified as bearish must be explicitly added
propensity for cold water surfing to the list of excluded locations. This forces the algorithm to
redistribute the budget to markets with compatible surf culture (such as Japan, USA or
Northern Europe), exchanging volume of followers for quality of potential customers.
3rd Problem:
●​ High BSV (Branded Search Volume) (many people search for the brand).
●​ CVR (Conversion Rate) drops specifically for beginners.
●​ Neutral/confused BSS (Brand Sentiment) in the comments (“Is this just for pros?”).
This scenario generally occurs in brands that rely heavily on history and
surfing legends, which can lead the potential client, in this case the beginner, to perceive the
brand as excessively cool or hardcore.
Despite there being a high volume of searches associated with the brand, the rate of
conversion of this segment is residual. Additionally, the dominant feeling is one of confusion,
since it is not clear whether the school is aimed exclusively at experienced surfers or whether
also welcomes beginners. This ambiguity, often reflected in the comments of
publications, tends to alienate this more inexperienced audience.
Optimizations:
1st – The isolated interest in “Surf” or “Polynesian Culture” is excessively
comprehensive for an international surf school. A user can identify with the
Saoloto vibe without ever leaving its home country. In international markets, the
Segmentation must therefore resort to Travel Intent Layering, crossing interest in “Surf”
with mandatory behaviors such as “Frequent International Travelers” or “Interest
in Travel to Portugal”.
This approach allows us to filter out the so-called “couch fans” and ensure that the narrative
of Samoan Legend is only delivered to users who, statistically, demonstrate
propensity and financial capacity to travel to school.
2nd – The iconography associated with “Warriors” and “Ancestral Legends” is creating a
psychological barrier to entry, implicitly suggesting that error, failure or lack of
dexterity are not welcome in the “tribe”. To mitigate this effect, it is recommended to
implementation of a content humanization strategy (The Smiling Warrior). This
involves creating an editorial line of videos (Reels/TikToks) and testimonials that
show real beginners falling, laughing and learning in a safe environment accompanied by
instructors.
By visually normalizing the learning process, reinforcing that “everything
warrior starts from scratch”, the perception of elitism is reduced and the school is validated with the
amateur audience, particularly in the comments section.
3rd – The current website, excessively focused on Saoloto’s philosophy and symbolism,
does not answer the practical doubts and critical insecurities of those who have never had contact with the
surfing (fear of the sea, technical difficulties, equipment, safety), leading to abandonment in
moment of decision. It is recommended to develop a Landing Page dedicated to
beginners (Zero-Friction Page), which replaces abstraction with clarity.
This page should deconstruct the experience step by step (“What will you learn in
your 1st class”), explicitly ensure that safety and equipment are included and
use reassuring language. The objective is for it to function as a “safe haven”
within the site, converting curiosity (high BSV) into trust and effective booking (CVR).
A/B Testing
As one of the services, aimed at the Portuguese market, is a
class subscription, the A/B test variable will be the price presentation format.
Regardless of whether the user selects a 3, 6 or 12 month package, the possibility
test is whether the monetary value of the service should be shown as a monthly fee or as
single payment.
The central metric will be the number of clicks on the chosen preference, allowing
identify which of the two presentations generates greater traction. The objective is to understand which
format that the public values most and, based on that, automatically adopt the option with
better CTR, reducing the number of clicks needed to convert.
In summary, the 360º knowledge that the team has about the
project. Although this is a fictitious exercise, the
main issues inherent to the pre-launch, launch and post-launch phases, having
these have been critically framed and, whenever possible, accompanied by proposals for
solution.
2.3.4.2.4 Results - Dashboard Structure
The dashboard was designed to monitor the performance of the
marketing throughout the entire funnel. The structure is organized into five main sections, for
funnel phase, ensuring clear and organized reading.
●​ Section 1: Overview (General Performance)
This section presents an executive summary of the global state of marketing and
business, allowing you to quickly understand whether the strategy is aligned with the objectives.
Metrics included:
○​ Total Sales: Total number of sales generated in the analyzed period.
○​ CVR – Conversion Rate: Percentage of visitors who complete a
purchase.
○​ CAC – Customer Acquisition Cost: Average cost to acquire a new
customer, resulting from the division between investment in marketing and number of
new customers.
○​ CLV – Customer Lifetime Value: Total value expected per customer throughout
of your relationship with the brand.
○​ Retention/NPS: Indicators of quality of experience and loyalty (included
when data exists).
Section Objective:
Provide a macro view of marketing efficiency, traffic quality
and the profitability of customer acquisition.
●​ Section 2: TOFU – Awareness and Cultural Reach
Focused on the top of the funnel, this section analyzes brand awareness and
impact of cultural content, a central element of Saoloto’s positioning.
Metrics included:
○​ CCR – Cultural Content Reach: Total reach of cultural content
associated with Samoan roots.
○​ BSV – Branded Search Volume: Direct search volume by terms
related to the brand, an indicator of spontaneous awareness.
○​ Total Impressions: Total number of impressions generated in the main
social platforms.
○​ Cultural Engagement Rate: Percentage of interactions generated by
cultural contents.
○​ New Visitors (Website): Number of new visitors to the website, useful for
realize the effectiveness of awareness campaigns.
Section Objective:
Assess brand visibility, cultural impact of content and brand growth
spontaneous search.
●​ Section 3: MOFU – Consideration and Community
This phase analyzes the behavior of users who have already shown interest,
measuring depth of content consumption and community generation capacity.
Metrics included:
○​ AToP – Average Time on Page: Average time that users
remain on each relevant page.
○​ Scroll Depth: Percentage of content actually viewed per page.
○​ CTR (Campaigns / Key Content): Indicator of effectiveness of
messages in generating actions.
○​ CGR – Community Growth Rate: Community growth rate in
loyalty channels (newsletter, Reddit, private groups).
○​ Lead Capture Rate: Percentage of visitors who leave contact or
register.
Section Objective:
Measure real interest, quality of website experience and ability to convert
users into community members.
Section 4: BOFU – Conversion and Value
Critical zone of the funnel, dedicated to analyzing commercial performance and efficiency in
value generation.
Metrics included:
○​ CR – Conversion Rate: Rate of conversion of visitors into buyers.
○​ Checkout Abandonment Rate: Percentage of users who initiate the
checkout but do not complete the purchase.
○​ CAC – Customer Acquisition Cost: Reevaluated specifically at this stage
for a clear perception of profitability.
○​ ROI: Indicator of total economic return, after subtracting the investment.
○​ CLV – Customer Lifetime Value: Key metric to evaluate the
sustainability and longevity of the relationship with the customer.
Section Objective:
Ensure that the commercial structure is efficient, identify leak points in the journey
purchasing process and analyze the economic value generated.
●​ Section 5: Retention & Loyalty
A post-purchase section that complements the analysis, allowing you to understand
longevity, repetition and customer loyalty.
Metrics included:
○​ Repeat Purchase Rate: Percentage of customers who purchase again.
○​ Average Time Between Purchases: Average interval between successive purchases.
○​ NPS – Net Promoter Score: Indicator of satisfaction and probability of
recommendation.
Section Objective:
Assess the brand’s ability to generate lasting relationships, promote repetition and
build an active and loyal community.
3. Conclusion
The development of this project, focused on the creation and go-to-market strategy
of Saoloto Surf School, allowed us to follow a complex itinerary that transformed a
initial idea into a tangible, differentiated and operationally viable business model. Ao
Throughout the various stages of this Business Case, we sought not only to structure a school of
surfing, but building a brand with soul, capable of responding to the challenges of a market
saturated through a unique value proposition: the fusion between Samoan spiritual heritage and
the hospitality of Costa da Caparica.
The initial phase of strategic diagnosis proved to be fundamental to support all
subsequent decisions. The application of the 4C’s framework allowed us to deconstruct the scenario
current competitive environment, where a clear saturation of the offer focused on performance was identified
technology and mass tourism. The validation of Costa da Caparica as a physical location,
to the detriment of Cascais, it was not just a geographical choice, but a decision to
positioning: authenticity, wild nature and space for
grow, moving the brand away from congested urban centers where the surfing "vibe" is lost
in excessive commercialization. This analysis confirmed that although there are 678 schools
surfing in Portugal, there is a blue ocean for anyone who sets out to sell not just lessons,
but belonging.
The construction of the brand identity, materialized in the Brand Guidelines, was the
turning point that allowed Saoloto to stop being a theoretical project and come to life
own. The definition of the name "Saoloto" (Freedom) and the motto "Where the Waves Carve
Family" served as a compass for all tactical choices. As we focus on branding
human and community, we respond directly to the pain identified in our
personas.
For Lukas, the experienced traveler, we offer the cultural depth that is missing in
commercial schools; For Kelly, the independent woman, we guarantee safety and security
welcoming a non-intimidating environment; and for Duarte, the local young man, we created a
space of formation and identity. This psychographic segmentation, more than demographic,
ensures that Saoloto communicates with emotional relevance, a critical factor in converting
interest in loyalty in a market where the barrier to entry for the consumer is, many times,
Sometimes, the fear of not belonging.
The Marketing Mix strategy (7Ps) and the communication ecosystem (POEM)
demonstrated the ability to operationalize this philosophical vision. The decision to adopt a
Competitive Pricing strategy in the Upper-Middle segment, supported by a strong
digital presence and partnerships with influencers such as Teresa Bonvalot and Hunter Jones,
positions Saoloto as an affordable premium offering.
We don't sell the lowest price, we sell the highest perceived value: the down payment
in a tribe. The structure of the ecosystem, from the top of the funnel with lifestyle content and
storytelling (like the "Big Z" narrative) to conversion via Google Ads and Website
optimized, proves that the brand is prepared to capture, nurture and convert leads in a
efficient. The focus on video (Reels) and social proof (UGC) reflects an understanding
deep understanding of the consumption habits of the Millennial and Gen Z generations, ensuring that the brand
keeps it relevant and visible where consumer attention currently resides.
From a feasibility and management point of view, the plan presented is realistic and
conservative. The Build-Up budget strategy, focused on the essentials for the start-up, combined with
to a rigorous control panel (Dashboard), allows constant monitoring of health
of the business.
Defining clear SMART objectives, from initial awareness to conversion rate
retention in Surf Camps, guarantees that management will not be done by intuition, but by data.
We are prepared to monitor Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) and Lifetime
Value (LTV) from day one, allowing agile adjustments if the market reacts appropriately
different than expected.
Cross-strategies (SWOT) also demonstrated that Saoloto has
planned resilience, with responses prepared for seasonality or
aggressiveness of the competition, such as betting on packages for "Wave Poolers" or
loyalty through quality of service.
More than a business plan, this project presents a cultural manifesto.
In an increasingly digital and isolated world, where surfing runs the risk of becoming just
yet another fitness industry, Saoloto Surf School proposes a return to its origins. Proposes
May the sea once again be a place of worship and connection.
The conclusion we reached is that the viability of this project does not only lie in the
quality of its waves or its boards, but in the strength of the community that aims to
to create. If the market demands performance, Saoloto delivers experience; if the market sells
isolation, Saoloto delivers family.
In short, Saoloto Surf School meets all the strategic, financial and
operations to assert itself as a reference player in Costa da Caparica and, on average,
term, in the national panorama of surf tourism. The work developed here proves that it is
possible to combine the passion for the sea with the rigor of marketing management, creating a brand that is,
simultaneously a profitable business and a spiritual refuge. We are ready to open
doors, enter the water and begin to carve, wave by wave, our family.
